clue.text: Pirate can't do this with mermaid, as some may 'ave said

indicators.note: the dropped H of 'ave tells us the phrase is spoken, H-less, in a casual accent

parts.note: a mermaid has a tail and no feet, so you cannot count her feet; said with the H dropped it is the sound wanted

explanation.surface: A buccaneer muses, in a rough accent, on something he cannot manage with a mermaid.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken H-less, 'count 'er feet' sounds like the answer; Chambers allows the second syllable to rhyme with 'feet'.
explanation.definitionFit: To pirate goods is to copy them without permission, i.e. to fake or forge them.

clue.text: Philosophical approach, getting really ill before right email's gone off

indicators.note: the first piece is placed ahead of the rest

parts.note: a patient who is critical is gravely ill

indicators.note: something gone off has gone bad or wrong, so these letters are disordered

parts.note: the possessive 's supplies its S as fodder here, so all six letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: A thinker develops a philosophy while very sick, once the latest message has gone astray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'really ill' looks like part of the surface's sick thinker, but it is the synonym piece; 'getting' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Critical realism is a named school of thought in philosophy of science and perception, so it is a philosophical approach.

clue.text: Puma might have a savoury taste

indicators.note: the words 'Puma might' are said to have, i.e. contain, the answer within them

explanation.surface: A big cat's flesh might taste meaty and pleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: Umami is the Japanese-named fifth basic taste, the savoury quality of broths and meat.

clue.text: Song with (shh!) a million chords left out

indicators.note: letters that are out are put out of place, so the preceding words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tune whose many chords have been dropped, played quietly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' signals the anagram of SHH plus A MILLION CHORDS LEFT; 'left' looks like part of 'left out', but its letters are fodder. 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a well-known late-18th-century English love ballad about a girl from a district of London.

clue.text: Weird sorcerer's ferret

parts.note: rum is an old British word for odd or strange
a mage is a magician or sorcerer; the 's is a link

explanation.surface: An odd wizard's pet weasel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ferret' looks like the animal but is the verb, to hunt about.
explanation.definitionFit: To ferret about is to search busily through things, i.e. to root around among them.

clue.text: Dig up 12's mark given to wine in summer abroad

indicators.note: the cross and the wine together go inside the summer word

parts.note: ete is the French word for summer

indicators.note: the mark is set beside the wine, ahead of it

parts.note: a voter, the answer to 12, marks a ballot with a cross, X
cava is a Spanish sparkling wine

explanation.surface: Someone digs up a ballot mark, plus some wine, during a summer holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: To excavate a site is to dig it up or unearth what lies beneath.

clue.text: Sum of money making lonely content once

parts.note: the inner letters of lonely are O, N, E, L, read as one L, i.e. one pound, which this sum made in old British money

explanation.surface: An amount of cash that once made an isolated person happy.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1971 British money had twenty shillings to the pound (L, from Latin libra), so this sum once made 'one L', the content of 'lonely'.
explanation.definitionFit: In pre-decimal British currency this many shillings made one pound, a definite amount of money.

clue.text: Hindu magistrate at university in desert

indicators.note: the magistrate and university go inside the desert word

parts.note: to rat is to desert or betray one's side

indicators.note: the university letter sits right after the magistrate

parts.note: JP stands for Justice of the Peace, a British magistrate

explanation.surface: An Indian official is at college in the middle of a wilderness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'desert' looks like a noun (sand) but is the verb, to rat.
explanation.definitionFit: Rajputs are a Hindu warrior caste of northern India, so one is a Hindu.

clue.text: Refuse rebid, changing to spades

indicators.note: the spade letter is added on to the end
the bridge word rebid is changed, i.e. rearranged

parts.note: S is the card abbreviation for spades

explanation.surface: A bridge player declines to bid again, switching to spades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb at bridge but is the noun, rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Debris is scattered rubbish or wreckage, i.e. refuse.

clue.text: Wind up having sex in a way-out place?

indicators.note: the sex word goes inside the gate

parts.note: a gate is a place you go out through, a way out
it is a coy word for sex

explanation.surface: Having sex somewhere outlandish might get people riled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'way-out' looks like 'eccentric' but literally means an exit.
explanation.definitionFit: To wind someone up is to provoke them, to stir them up or agitate them.

clue.text: China possesses revolutionary weapon

indicators.note: the friend word holds the revolutionary inside it

parts.note: china is Cockney rhyming slang (china plate) for mate
Che Guevara is the archetypal revolutionary

explanation.surface: The Chinese state owns a revolutionary arms system.
explanation.walkthrough: China (china plate) is Cockney rhyming slang for mate, a friend; the capital C disguises it as the country.
explanation.definitionFit: A machete is a large broad-bladed knife, which can be used as a weapon.

clue.text: Proper pair treated a first-time mother

parts.note: prim means proper or prudish

indicators.note: treated means processed or worked on, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A respectable couple care for a woman having her first baby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treated' rearranges PAIR into IPAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Primipara is the medical term for a woman giving birth for the first time.

clue.text: Active constituent of vodka or (tenuously) even rum, originally

indicators.note: originally points to the starts of the following words

explanation.surface: The chemical that does the work in vodka or perhaps rum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Active constituent' reads like chemistry, but it means an electorate member who uses their vote.
explanation.definitionFit: A voter is a member of a constituency who actually takes part by voting.

clue.text: Drinks kid hasn't finished

indicators.note: the word lacks its finish, its final letter

parts.note: to kid is to tease

explanation.surface: A child hasn't drunk up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kid' looks like a child but is the verb, to tease.
explanation.definitionFit: Teas are cups of tea, i.e. drinks; also afternoon meals.

clue.text: Wife leaves grant aid outside of that detailed for lung disease

indicators.note: the shortened aid word goes around the other piece
detailed means with its tail cut off, losing its last letter

parts.note: to assist is to aid

indicators.note: the wife letter leaves the grant word

parts.note: to bestow is to grant

explanation.surface: With the spouse gone, a grant pays for a disease more specifically described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' takes W out of BESTOW for BESTO; 'detailed' cuts ASSIST to ASSIS, which goes 'outside of' BESTO; 'that' points back to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Asbestosis is the scarring of lung tissue caused by inhaling asbestos fibres.

clue.text: Whip yellow topping for pudding to be eaten by young family member

indicators.note: the yellow piece and the top letter go inside the family member

parts.note: a scion is a descendant, a younger member of a family
or is gold or yellow in heraldry

indicators.note: the topping is the uppermost, first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Beat some yellow cream for a dessert that a child will eat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whip' looks like the cookery verb; it is a noun, the biblical scourge ('chastise you with scorpions').
explanation.definitionFit: A scorpion was a barbed whip or scourge, as in Rehoboam's threat in the Bible.

clue.text: See 3
Dark blue shoe?

definitions.meaning: ... blue is a dark navy shade, and ... University's rowers are the Dark Blues
a style of laced leather shoe

explanation.definitionFit: Oxford names both a dark navy colour and a classic laced brogue-style shoe.

clue.text: Setter eating his first suet pudding is essential viewing

annotationWithheld.why: Setter eating his first suet pudding is essential viewing (4-3): only parse is ME round S + anagram of SUET, where S is the first of 'Setter', so 'Setter' gives both ME and S
annotationWithheld.clue: Setter eating his first suet pudding is essential viewing

clue.text: What may be produced from ten plus one: a product of 11?

indicators.note: produced from means made out of these letters by rearrangement

explanation.surface: A newborn emerges from arithmetic, in a riddle about a first-time mother.
explanation.walkthrough: 11 is PRIMIPARA, a woman with her first child, whose product is a newborn; 'plus' is only a link joining TEN and ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A neonate is a newborn baby, which is what a first-time mother delivers.

clue.text: See 3
Amateur given place on staff

indicators.note: in a down answer the first piece sits on top of the second

parts.note: to lay is to place or put down
to man a post is to staff it

explanation.surface: A non-professional is given a post among the employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'staff' looks like a noun, workers, but is the verb, to man.
explanation.definitionFit: A layman is a non-expert, someone without professional training, i.e. an amateur.

clue.text: Endless failure not for everyone — the rest developed talent

indicators.note: what remains is developed, i.e. worked into a new order
U is the British film certificate for universal viewing, suitable for everyone, so the U is removed
endless means losing its end, the last letter

explanation.surface: A failure that never ends, unsuitable for all, still grows into a gift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' cuts FAILURE to FAILUR; removing U leaves FAILR, which 'the rest developed' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Flair is a natural aptitude or knack, a talent for something.

clue.text: Use of weapons in second part of clue?

parts.note: wordplay is the part of a crossword clue that builds the answer

explanation.surface: A clue setter's joke about weapons being used in the latter half.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link: S and WORDPLAY simply sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Swordplay is fencing, the skilful use of swords.

clue.text: Block cross, as a result

parts.note: read as wordplay, the answer means 'dam' written upwards in this down light, which gives mad, i.e. cross

explanation.surface: Barricade the junction because of it.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer itself is the wordplay, DAM reversed ('up', in a down answer) making MAD, angry; 'as a result' links.
explanation.definitionFit: To dam up a river is to block its flow with a barrier.

clue.text: Fruit from Madeira is insect-ridden

indicators.note: the answer is taken from within the string of words that follows

explanation.surface: Dried grapes from the Portuguese island are full of bugs.
explanation.definitionFit: Raisins are dried grapes, a kind of fruit.

clue.text: I tucked into God-awful starter, something pungent

indicators.note: the letter is slipped inside the other pieces

parts.note: Ammon is the Egyptian god, also called Amun

indicators.note: the starter of a word is its first letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: I hide inside a dreadful first course, something that reeks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'God-awful' reads as one word, but splits into AMMON (God) and A, the starter of 'awful'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ammonia is a colourless gas with a sharp, choking smell.

clue.text: Outstanding peer in Brussels?

parts.note: peer is read as pee-er, one who urinates; the famous Brussels fountain statue is a little boy doing so, out in the open

explanation.surface: A distinguished nobleman visiting the Belgian capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peer' suggests a lord, but read as 'pee-er' it is the little bronze boy urinating into the fountain basin in Brussels.
explanation.definitionFit: The bronze fountain statue of a urinating boy is the best-known landmark of Brussels.
